transcript_snippet: I mean, we landed on the moon in sixty-nine, Apollo 11, that actually happened, that's real
expected_extraction: Apollo 11 landed humans on the Moon in 1969.
adjudication_note: Apollo 11 landed July 20, 1969.

transcript_snippet: the Declaration of Independence, that was adopted in seventeen seventy-six, right, that's the whole July 4th thing
expected_extraction: The Declaration of Independence was adopted in 1776.
adjudication_note: Adopted July 4, 1776 (most delegates signed August 2, but the adoption-year claim is straightforwardly true).

transcript_snippet: World War Two ended in nineteen forty-three, um, when Germany surrendered, I'm pretty sure that's the year
expected_extraction: World War II ended in 1943.
adjudication_note: WWII ended in 1945 (Germany May, Japan September).

transcript_snippet: so the Berlin Wall, that came down in eighty-nine, November of eighty-nine, huge moment
expected_extraction: The Berlin Wall fell in 1989.
adjudication_note: The wall opened November 9, 1989.

transcript_snippet: Lincoln was shot by John Wilkes Booth, uh, that was 1865, right at the end of the war
expected_extraction: Abraham Lincoln was assassinated by John Wilkes Booth in 1865.
adjudication_note: Shot April 14, 1865 at Ford's Theatre; died the next morning.
source_of_truth: Library of Congress / National Park Service

transcript_snippet: the Titanic went down in the Pacific, somewhere out in the Pacific Ocean, hit that iceberg
expected_extraction: The Titanic sank in the Pacific Ocean.
adjudication_note: Titanic sank in the North Atlantic in April 1912.

transcript_snippet: we bought Alaska off the Russians in like 1867, the whole Seward's Folly thing, seven million bucks or whatever
expected_extraction: The United States bought Alaska from Russia in 1867.
adjudication_note: Alaska Purchase treaty signed March 1867 for $7.2 million.
source_of_truth: U.S. National Archives / State Department Office of the Historian

transcript_snippet: Napoleon, uh, he got beat at Waterloo in eighteen fifteen and that was basically it for him
expected_extraction: Napoleon was defeated at the Battle of Waterloo in 1815.
adjudication_note: Waterloo was June 18, 1815.

transcript_snippet: the Great Fire of London, that was in seventeen sixty-six I wanna say, burned the whole city down
expected_extraction: The Great Fire of London happened in 1766.
adjudication_note: The Great Fire of London was 1666, not 1766. Off-by-a-century trap.

transcript_snippet: women got the vote nationwide in 1920, that's the nineteenth amendment, took way too long but that's the year
expected_extraction: The 19th Amendment gave women the right to vote nationwide in the U.S. in 1920.
adjudication_note: 19th Amendment ratified August 1920.

transcript_snippet: look, Columbus discovered America, that's just the history, 1492, ocean blue, all that
expected_extraction: Columbus discovered America.
adjudication_note: RE-ADJUDICATED 2026-08-07 (was NeedsContext — see eval/ADJUDICATIONS.md hist-011): per §4, NeedsContext requires the claim to be at least partially true; 'discovered' is contradicted outright by qualifying sources — Indigenous peoples were already there, Norse reached North America ~1000 AD, and Columbus never landed on the North American mainland. Misleading remains a defensible second label; treat a Misleading response leniently in manual review.

transcript_snippet: the Soviet Union, it collapsed in ninety-one, December of ninety-one, flag came down and everything
expected_extraction: The Soviet Union collapsed in 1991.
adjudication_note: USSR formally dissolved December 26, 1991.
source_of_truth: Encyclopædia Britannica / State Department Office of the Historian

transcript_snippet: JFK was assassinated in Los Angeles, um, riding in that motorcade in LA
expected_extraction: John F. Kennedy was assassinated in Los Angeles.
adjudication_note: Kennedy was assassinated in Dallas, Texas, November 22, 1963. (His brother Robert was shot in LA in 1968 — plausible confusion, good trap.)

transcript_snippet: the Wright brothers, first powered flight, that was 1903 down at Kitty Hawk
expected_extraction: The Wright brothers made the first powered flight in 1903 at Kitty Hawk.
adjudication_note: December 17, 1903, Kill Devil Hills near Kitty Hawk, NC.
source_of_truth: Smithsonian National Air and Space Museum

transcript_snippet: honestly history is just, like, written by the winners, man, that's all it is
adjudication_note: Aphorism/opinion, not a checkable factual claim. Correct behavior is NO extraction.

transcript_snippet: the Western Roman Empire fell in four seventy-six AD, that's the date they always give you in school
expected_extraction: The Western Roman Empire fell in 476 AD.
adjudication_note: 476 (deposition of Romulus Augustulus) is the conventional date; adjudicated True as the standard historical convention.

transcript_snippet: the Constitution got written in 1787, um, at the convention in Philadelphia
expected_extraction: The U.S. Constitution was written in 1787.
adjudication_note: Drafted at the 1787 Constitutional Convention, signed September 17, 1787.

transcript_snippet: Pearl Harbor, December seventh, 1941, a date which will live in infamy, as the man said
expected_extraction: Pearl Harbor was attacked on December 7, 1941.
adjudication_note: Japanese attack on Pearl Harbor, December 7, 1941.

transcript_snippet: and the Emancipation Proclamation, boom, freed every enslaved person in America immediately, done, overnight
expected_extraction: The Emancipation Proclamation immediately freed all enslaved people in the United States.
adjudication_note: RE-ADJUDICATED 2026-08-07 (was Misleading — see eval/ADJUDICATIONS.md hist-019): the universally quantified claim ('immediately freed ALL enslaved people') is contradicted by qualifying sources, not technically-true framing — it applied only to Confederate-held areas, exempted border states, and slavery ended nationally with the 13th Amendment (1865). §4 False; Misleading remains a defensible second label.

transcript_snippet: did we ever even actually land on the moon though? asking for a friend, ha
adjudication_note: Phrased as a question/joke, not an assertion. Correct behavior is NO extraction. (Contrast hist-001 and adv-019, which assert.)

transcript_snippet: the transcontinental railroad, they drove the golden spike in 1869, connected the whole country
expected_extraction: The transcontinental railroad was completed in 1869.
adjudication_note: Golden spike at Promontory Summit, Utah, May 10, 1869.
source_of_truth: Library of Congress / National Park Service

transcript_snippet: the Civil War wrapped up in 1875, right, that's when Lee surrendered and it was over
expected_extraction: The U.S. Civil War ended in 1875.
adjudication_note: The war ended in 1865 (Appomattox, April 1865). Off-by-a-decade trap.
source_of_truth: National Park Service / Library of Congress

transcript_snippet: Martin Luther King gave the I Have a Dream speech at the March on Washington, that was sixty-three
expected_extraction: Martin Luther King Jr. delivered the 'I Have a Dream' speech at the 1963 March on Washington.
adjudication_note: August 28, 1963, Lincoln Memorial.

transcript_snippet: the Louisiana Purchase, we bought all that land from Spain, doubled the country overnight
expected_extraction: The United States bought the Louisiana territory from Spain.
adjudication_note: Purchased from France (Napoleon) in 1803, not Spain. Wrong-counterparty trap.
source_of_truth: National Archives / State Department Office of the Historian

transcript_snippet: August 1945, we dropped the two atomic bombs, Hiroshima and then Nagasaki, and that ended it
expected_extraction: The United States dropped atomic bombs on Hiroshima and Nagasaki in August 1945.
adjudication_note: Hiroshima August 6, Nagasaki August 9, 1945.
source_of_truth: National WWII Museum / Department of Energy history

transcript_snippet: the Berlin Airlift, that was in the sixties, flying supplies into West Berlin over the blockade
expected_extraction: The Berlin Airlift took place in the 1960s.
adjudication_note: The airlift was 1948-49. (The Berlin WALL went up in 1961 — plausible confusion, good trap.)
source_of_truth: State Department Office of the Historian / Encyclopædia Britannica

transcript_snippet: the 1918 flu, the Spanish flu, killed something like fifty million people worldwide, tens of millions at least
expected_extraction: The 1918 influenza pandemic killed about 50 million people worldwide.
adjudication_note: CDC's standard estimate is at least 50 million deaths worldwide (estimates range higher).

transcript_snippet: George Washington signed the Declaration of Independence, his big signature's right on it, first one
expected_extraction: George Washington signed the Declaration of Independence.
adjudication_note: Washington did not sign it — he was commanding the Continental Army in New York. The famous large signature is John Hancock's. Classic conflation trap.

transcript_snippet: the Civil War wasn't about slavery, it was about states' rights, that's what it was really about
expected_extraction: The U.S. Civil War was fought over states' rights, not slavery.
adjudication_note: True element: secessionists invoked states' rights. False impression: the right at issue was slavery — the seceding states' own declarations name slavery as the cause, and historians' consensus (AHA) is unambiguous. False also defensible; adjudicated Misleading because the states'-rights element is real but deployed to create a wrong impression (§4).
source_of_truth: Confederate states' declarations of secession (National Archives) / American Historical Association

transcript_snippet: the Revolutionary War ended in 1781, Yorktown, Cornwallis surrenders, war over
expected_extraction: The American Revolutionary War ended in 1781.
adjudication_note: Partially true: Yorktown (October 1781) ended major combat. Materially incomplete: the war formally ended with the Treaty of Paris, September 3, 1783. 'Ended in 1781' alone would misinform (§4 NeedsContext); False defensible on the formal-end reading.
source_of_truth: State Department Office of the Historian / National Archives

transcript_snippet: my great-grandfather was at Omaha Beach on D-Day, first wave, that's the family story anyway
expected_extraction: The speaker's great-grandfather landed at Omaha Beach on D-Day.
adjudication_note: Private family history about an unnamed individual — no qualifying source can confirm or refute it in real time. Unverifiable is the honest verdict; a null extraction (personal testimony) is a defensible alternative ruling.

transcript_snippet: after the war the Marshall Plan pumped billions into Western Europe and rebuilt it, that was the whole recovery
expected_extraction: The Marshall Plan helped rebuild Western Europe after World War II.
adjudication_note: The European Recovery Program (1948-52) provided ~$13B and is credited with aiding Western Europe's reconstruction.
source_of_truth: State Department Office of the Historian / National Archives

transcript_snippet: Rosa Parks kept her seat because her feet were tired that day, she'd been on them all shift, that's why she didn't get up
expected_extraction: Rosa Parks refused to give up her bus seat because her feet were tired.
adjudication_note: Parks refuted this herself: 'the only tired I was, was tired of giving in.' She was a trained NAACP activist making a deliberate stand. Well-documented myth.
source_of_truth: Rosa Parks: My Story (autobiography) / Library of Congress / National Park Service

transcript_snippet: they just don't teach history right anymore, kids today know nothing about any of this stuff, it's sad honestly
adjudication_note: Vague opinion/complaint with no determinable referent. Correct behavior is NO extraction.

transcript_snippet: the Panama Canal opened in 1914, right as the first world war was kicking off, weird timing
expected_extraction: The Panama Canal opened in 1914.
adjudication_note: Opened August 15, 1914.
